scripts.objectives: Students will learn that umbrellas are made from waterproof material. They will understand why waterproof materials do not let water through.
facts: The umbrella cloth is waterproof, so rain rolls off instead of soaking in.
If the cloth could absorb water, you would still get wet underneath.
In Singapore's sudden rain, an umbrella keeps you dry on your walk to school.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that some materials can float on water. They will understand how floating materials help us in water.
facts: The kickboard is made of foam, which floats on the water's surface.
Floating materials stay near the top and do not sink down.
At Singapore swimming pools, kids hold a kickboard to stay afloat while learning to swim.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that glass is transparent. They will understand how transparent materials let us see through them.
facts: The window is made of glass, which is transparent so light passes through.
Transparent materials let us see what is on the other side clearly.
On the MRT, the clear windows let you watch HDB blocks zoom past on your ride.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that rubber is flexible. They will understand that flexible materials can bend or stretch without breaking.
facts: A rubber band is flexible and can stretch far without snapping.
Flexible materials can bend back into shape after you let go.
At the wet market in Singapore, sellers use rubber bands to tie up bags of food.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that metal is strong. They will understand that strong materials can hold heavy loads without breaking.
facts: The railing is made of metal, which is strong and does not break easily.
Strong materials can hold weight when many people lean or grab them.
In Singapore HDB blocks, sturdy metal railings keep everyone safe on the stairs.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that raincoats use waterproof plastic. They will understand why waterproof clothing keeps us dry.
facts: A raincoat is made of plastic that water cannot pass through.
Because it does not absorb water, your clothes stay dry inside.
Delivery riders in Singapore wear raincoats to keep dry during heavy showers.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that a ruler can be both flexible and transparent. They will understand that one object can have more than one property.
facts: A plastic ruler can bend a little, showing it is flexible.
Many rulers are clear, so you can see the lines you are measuring.
In Singapore classrooms, a see-through ruler helps you draw neat lines over your work.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that slippers are flexible and waterproof. They will understand how these properties make them useful.
facts: Slippers are made of rubber that bends easily as you walk.
The rubber is waterproof, so it does not soak up puddles.
Singaporeans love wearing slippers to the void deck or to buy food nearby.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that some materials absorb water and are not waterproof. They will understand the difference between absorbing and repelling water.
facts: A sponge soaks up water, so it is not waterproof.
Materials that absorb water get heavy and wet when soaked.
At home in Singapore, a sponge helps you wipe up spilled drinks quickly.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that some materials sink in water. They will understand that heavy, dense objects do not float.
facts: A metal coin sinks straight to the bottom of the water.
Sinking objects do not stay on the surface like floating ones do.
If you drop a Singapore coin into a fountain, it sinks and rests at the bottom.
